title: Angry with God
hook: Job and the psalmists were allowed to be angry with God (Psalm 22:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dead. Your line was it still counts. Did you say anything aloud? Today, the hardest place some people's anger goes: upward. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the first words of Psalm 22. Not a hymn of thanks. Not a calm reflection. A cry, aimed straight at God, asking why. It sits inside the Bible's own prayer book, kept and prayed. Somebody decided that this belonged in scripture, accusation and all. It wasn't filed away as an embarrassing moment or softened into something more polite. It was left exactly as raw as it is, for anyone who would ever need those words. Today: angry with God.
screen: `WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?` → `A CRY, NOT A HYMN.` → `KEPT IN THE PRAYER BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the psalm keeps going. Psalm 22 goes on: "why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring. Not whispering. The psalm does move, later, toward trust and praise, but it doesn't skip the roar to get there. The same opening line appears in another place too: in Matthew and Mark, Jesus cries it from the cross. Second, Job. Job loses his children, his wealth, his health, and his friends arrive with explanations. Job refuses them. He says: "I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul." He spends chapter after chapter demanding that God answer him. Third, the surprise at the end. When God finally speaks, out of the whirlwind, Job is pressed hard with questions. But as the book closes, God's anger turns on the friends who defended God so neatly: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The one who complained is the one who spoke rightly. Readers differ about what exactly that means. One reading: honest anger, brought to God, counts as a kind of faithfulness. Pretending does not. Fourth, the prophet Habakkuk opens his book the same way: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Again, it's kept, as scripture. Some people who pray hear these texts as a permission. For people who don't, there's still something here: the anger at how things went, at loss, at unfairness, is allowed to be said out loud, rather than buried. Honest is allowed.
screen: `THE WORDS OF MY ROARING.` · `I WILL NOT REFRAIN MY MOUTH.` · `JOB SPOKE RIGHTLY.` · `HOW LONG SHALL I CRY?` · then, large: `HONEST IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath come and go. Find one honest complaint, something about your life that seems unfair, or a loss that never made sense. Don't tidy it. If God is part of your life, you can say it to God, plainly, the way the psalm does: why? If not, say it to life, or to the night sky, or just to the room. Say it once, aloud or under your breath. Then stay in the quiet that follows. Nothing has to answer. The bell holds the time.
Angry with God. The honest complaint the psalms, Job and the prophets carry straight to God, and that scripture keeps. Today's word.
Your line: honest is allowed. Today, when the polite version starts forming, in prayer or in conversation, try saying the true one instead. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the psalms of lament, including Psalm 22, and some teachers in both traditions point to Job and the lament psalms as a model for bringing anger and complaint honestly to God.

notes: Job 42:7 is addressed to Eliphaz about him and his two friends; voiced as 'the friends'. Confirm.
'Readers have argued for a long time about what exactly that means' is a soft claim about interpretation history; a Keeper may prefer 'readers differ'.
Psalm 22 is numbered 22:2 in Hebrew for the opening cry (the superscription is verse 1). Original note cites 'Psalm 22' without a verse. Confirm Hebrew pointing and pronunciation.
Job 7:11 KJV begins 'Therefore I will not refrain'; the quotation starts at 'I will'. Confirm.
'Kept and prayed' in the hook is a general description of the Psalter's use; confirm acceptable under the claims rule.

Editor pass: hook said Psalm 22 sits 'in the middle' of the Psalter (it doesn't) and 'kept, copied and sung'; now 'inside... kept and prayed'. The teach and a myth item implied God never rebukes Job, though the whirlwind speeches (38–41) press him hard; the teach now says so, and the myth item now tests the friends' verdict instead. 'Christians know this line', 'readers have argued for a long time' and 'for people who pray, these texts are a permission' softened.
